title: Frank Painia's friendship, generosity and the Dew Drop's decline
summary: Tex wrote Painia's ad copy and received a suit in 1953; Painia swapped talent with Charlie Rosenthal in Texas; the Dew Drop today is run down.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: It is. It's still there. It is. Okay. It's still there. In fact, I spoke there for Black History Week, round about, I think about maybe about six years ago. And then, last year, I went with my wife and several other friends. They had a big Mardi Gras fair, promoted by one of the outstanding lady clubs here in the city of New Orleans. So, they still got things going on down in Poland and Dauphine. It's not just an army base. They have enough facility and space where you can go there and have a party or enjoy yourself and have a good time. And I only wish getting back to Frank Pena. I wish he was still alive today because he became one of my very, very dear friends. And he would always call me to help write some of his newspaper continuity. When he didn't feel like putting it together, I wrote some of the copy for him to put it in the Louisiana Weekly, Pittsburgh Courier, or even in the Informer Sentinel. And then, when it came to putting it on the radio, I wrote whatever was on my program, I wrote the continuity for it for Frank Pena. And that's what he liked about me. I tell you, in fact, Frank Pena liked me so much until Christmas 1953. He called me. He said, Tex, come up, I want to see you. When I hit the door, Frank had a brand new suit hanging there waiting for me. First time other than myself buying my own suit, somebody gave me a suit for a present. That was Frank Pena, and I'll forget that.
Did he treat a lot of people like that? Was he very generous?

Well, he was generous to a lot of people. Frank was a likable individual who just cared for people, and he just liked to get involved. And I was thinking about, I had a meeting with Frank Pena and Rosenthal from out of Port Arthur, Texas. I'm trying to think of Rosenthal. He had a theater and a nightclub, and he used to come here and talk to Frank Pena all the time. Sometimes Frank would send some of his talent over there to Orange, Texas, rather. Charlie Rosenthal was his name. Very nice man. I hope he's still alive. He was a guy who, he and Frank Pena were the very best of friends, and they took a liking to each other, and they would swap talent from time to time. People would, Earl King would probably leave the Dew Drop and go over to the Orange, Texas, and play either Smile or Lewis. Otherwise, they helped to keep the black experience, entertainment experience alive. And I like that. But today it's a different kind of ball game because most of those clubs, the, the, uh, Blue Drop is not what it used to be. It's a shadow of its former self. There's no more live entertainment there, I think. Uh, um, they had live entertainment there sometimes. Last year, just a temporary thing. Uh, but it was not the glory days of yesteryear with the big name talent that, uh, Frank Pena used to promote. Uh, the club is kind of run down. There's no place to park. Yeah. Like you could do in the forties and early forties and fifties. Everybody has an automobile nowadays. More people are living in the project now. And then you have a lot of broken down cars parked in the neighborhood. Uh, then, uh, your dope addicts, uh, uh, are now promenading all over the neighborhood now. And it's kind of dangerous out there. Uh, uh, you don't want to be caught in that neighborhood when it's getting dark. Yeah. It's, it, it, it's sad to say. But you will never see the dew drop of yesteryear again, like when it was in its glory, when Frank Pena was living. You will never see that. But you will always have the name of the dew drop whenever anybody get ready to write the history of jazz, blues, and big name entertainment of the South. And Frank Pena and the dew drop has to be mentioned in these articles, no doubt about it.
